To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the antiproliterative activity of human IFN is mediated by a specific receptor which binds the IFN molecule and that the binding is saturable, reversible, and specific.
the Daudi cell line has been shown to contain a population of cells that are resistant to the growth inhibitory effects of IFN-alpha, but that retain the ability to bind IFN.
the Daudi lymphoma cells have been isolated which bind IFN and that the initial peak of binding is either absent or reduced with the IFN-resistant cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation and characterization of Daudi cell variants that are resistant to the biological actions of human IFNs.
the isolation of Daudi cells resistant to human alpha interferon (IFNa).
the isolation of Daudi cells which have been transformed to a state where they possess specific IFN receptors and have been rendered sensitive to the antiprotective action of human IFN.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DIF8 and possibly DIF9 cells are defective in the initial phase of IFN-alpha receptor binding, whereas DIF3 cells have normal IFN binding.
the phenotype of DIF8 cells is due to an alteration in the receptor activation process and not to a change in receptor binding.
the phenotype of the IFN-resistant cells may reflect a defect in receptor function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

DIF3 cells possess IFN receptors identical to those of the parental IFN-sensitive Daudi cells, that DIF8 cells possess IFN binding sites but are deficient in receptor activation and that DIF9 cells possess a defect in IFN binding.
DIF3, which is resistant to IFN-alpha 1 and IFN-alpha 5, is defective in receptor activation whereas DIF8 and -9, which are resistant to IFN alpha 2 and -8, are defective in receptor binding.
the DIF3 cells have a receptor which binds all IFN-alpha subspeces equally well, whereas the DIF8 and the DIF9 cells have a receptor with a defect in the binding of IFN-alpha subspece 2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a novel and robust approach to identify and characterize novel IFN-alpha subspecificity in human cells.
the Daudi cells are not resistant to the antiviral action of IFN.
the initial binding of IFN to the cell surface is a critical step in the activation of the antiproliterative action of the interferon and the antiviral action of the interferons.
